chapter: Bill Robinson and Chuck and Chuckles
title: Stopping the show at the RKO Palace and Robinson's birthday cake
summary: Chuck and Chuckles stop the show after Peg Leg Bates; the manager tells Robinson he pays them $500 a week, and Robinson invites them for birthday cake.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: -- I hadn't seen Mr. Bill Bojangles Robinson till up to that time, see. He was having like his 52nd birthday, I think it was, at the RKO Palace in Boston, and I was wearing a derby at that time. We had become Chuck and Chuckles and so forth. I don't think he knew about that, because we didn't have the Chuck and Chuckles name at the time I met him, see. I was just Shorty, see. But the thing about it, he didn't know where I was from. He didn't know I was from the south or anything, and we got up there and he liked to play that game, you know. He liked to shoot pool. He made a complaint after he saw the show. Chuckles and I went out there and stopped the show. First it was Peg Leg Bates, he went out and he stopped the show. He was the one leg dancing fool. And then they had like Louise McCarroll, she sang, and the band played. Then they introduced Chuck and Chuckles. Chuck and Chuckles stopped the show. They had to do encores. So somehow -- he got indignant about that, you know. So he goes out front to the manager's office, and he says to the theater manager, "Chuck and Chuckles will have to go." So the theater manager said, "Well, now, I'm paying Bill Bojangles Robinson, the world's champion tap dancer, $5,000.00 a week, and I'm paying Chuck and Chuckles $500.00 a week," he said. "If you was to -- if anyone would have to go it would have to be Bill Bojangles Robinson, the world's champion tap dancer," see? So he didn't want to lose his job so he gets out of the manager's office in a hurry and

he come backstage, and he sends his valet over to Chuck and Chuckles' dressing room. And he wants to meet us. He wants to see who we are and what they do and who are they, this, that and the other. So that's what the valet did. He came and told us about Mr. Bojangles was having a birthday cake, getting ready to cut the cake, and he would like for us to come over, Chuck and Chuckles to come over, and have a slice. And wish him a happy birthday. So that's what we did. We went over there, he liked company, see, Bojangles, so he starts to talking and asking questions. "Who's your father," and, "Who's your mother," and, "Who's your uncle," and, "Who's your brother." "Why do you wear the derby?" "What kind of tap dancing is that you're doing?" Now, most tap dancers would say, "I'm tapping like Bill Bojangles Robinson," you know. And if he was satisfied that your tap dancing was good enough to tap dance like him, well, he would smile, you know, and say, "That's good. That's what you should always say." But I told him, I said, "Well, that's because of the office. They insisted that I wear a derby, on account of the Governor of New York State," you know. So he said, "I like you. I like the way you talk. Don't I know you?"
